Over 16,000 Supabase databases expose PII, passwords, auth tokens

UpGuard found more than 16,000 publicly accessible, misconfigured Supabase databases exposing sensitive data such as PII, plaintext passwords, and authentication tokens. The exposures stem largely from weak or missing row-level security policies and improper use of public keys, with AI-assisted development potentially increasing configuration mistakes.
KEY POINTS
  • 01UpGuard researchers found more than 16,000 misconfigured Supabase databases with readable tables exposing personal information, passwords, or authentication tokens.
  • 02The researchers analyzed about 300,000 domains showing signs of Supabase use and used accessible table schemas to infer the types of data exposed.
  • 03More than half of the exposed databases contained personally identifiable information, while smaller subsets contained passwords and authentication tokens.
  • 04Examples included a U.S. valet service with over 100,000 exposed customer records and a Canadian immigration service with nearly 5,000 user records, including 884 plaintext passwords.
  • 05UpGuard attributed the exposures to poor application security settings, including missing or ineffective row-level security policies and misuse of public keys.

UpGuard researchers found more than 16,000 misconfigured Supabase databases with readable tables exposing personally identifiable information, passwords, or authentication tokens. The researchers analyzed roughly 300,000 domains that appeared to use Supabase and examined accessible table schemas, including tables with names other than “users.” More than half of the exposed databases contained personal information, while smaller subsets exposed passwords and authentication tokens. UpGuard believes a very small portion of the exposed data included credit card information.

The exposed records affected organizations in multiple sectors and countries, including a U.S. valet service, a Canadian immigration service, an India-based adult creator platform, a Philippines-based OTP service, and an African government consulate. Examples included over 100,000 valet customer records, 884 plaintext passwords at the Canadian service, more than 100,000 private messages at the adult creator platform, and emergency housing locations in consulate records. UpGuard attributed the problem to poor application security configuration, including absent or ineffective row-level security policies and misuse of public keys. The researchers said AI-assisted development may increase the risk of such mistakes, though their scans did not establish that every exposed site was built using an AI coding agent.

  • The exposure was not limited to databases with a table named “users”; when that table was absent, researchers sometimes found that differently named tables were still accessible.
  • The affected organizations spanned unrelated sectors and regions, including valet parking, immigration services, adult-content platforms, SMS services, and a government consulate, indicating the configuration problem was not tied to one business type.
  • Although AI-assisted development accounts for more than 60% of newly created Supabase databases, UpGuard said its scans did not prove that every exposed site was created with an AI coding agent.
  • Some exposed data went beyond account details: researchers identified private messages, SMS communications, license plates, visit histories, emergency housing locations, and a small amount of apparent credit card data.
  • UpGuard said it notified application owners when deeper analysis identified significant exposure and directed Supabase users to the platform’s security advisors and API security guidance.

Researchers found more than 16,000 Supabase app databases that were set up so outsiders could read information that should have been private, including personal details, passwords, and account access codes. Affected services included a U.S. valet company, a Canadian immigration service, an Indian adult creator platform, a Philippines-based text-message service, and an African government consulate. This matters because exposed information can reveal people’s identities, private messages, payment details, locations, and ways to access accounts, potentially putting many people at risk.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a broad, concrete finding involving more than 16,000 exposed Supabase databases and sensitive data including PII, plaintext passwords, and authentication tokens. It is highly relevant to organizations using Supabase or reviewing AI-assisted application development, although the article does not report active exploitation.

Times Car confirms data breach affecting 6.6 million user accounts

Japanese car-sharing service Times Car confirmed that a cyberattack exposed personal data for about 6.6 million current and former users, including identity-document images and password hashes. Credit card data was not affected, and the company is notifying impacted customers while investigating the incident.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Times Car confirmed that a cyberattack compromised information associated with approximately 6.6 million current and former users, including members of its Times Business Service corporate program.
  • 02The company said unauthorized access to its systems began at the start of September and that it blocked the access on September 26.
  • 03Exposed data includes names, addresses, birth dates, telephone numbers, email addresses, driver’s license details, identity-document images, passwords, and linked service IDs.
  • 04Times Car said credit card information was not affected and that it has no current evidence that the stolen data has been distributed online.
  • 05The company is conducting a forensic investigation with an external expert and will notify affected customers in stages.

Japanese car-sharing service Times Car confirmed that a cyberattack compromised information tied to approximately 6.6 million current and former members, including members of its Times Business Service corporate program. The company said a third party accessed its systems at the beginning of September and that it blocked the unauthorized access on September 26. Times Car is operated by Times Mobility, part of the Park24 Group, and has said its services continue operating normally.

The exposed information includes names, addresses, birth dates, phone numbers, email addresses, driver’s license details, identity-verification document images, account passwords, and linked service IDs; corporate members’ department names may also be affected. Times Car said passwords were stored in a form that cannot be restored, but did not provide further details. The company said credit card information was unaffected and that it has no current evidence the stolen data has been distributed online, while it investigates with an external expert and notifies affected customers in stages.

  • The 6.6 million affected accounts include former members as well as current users, exceeding Times Car’s stated 4 million active members as of August 2026.
  • The exposed records may include images of driver’s licenses and other identity-verification documents, not only standard contact and account information.
  • Corporate-program members may have had their department names exposed in addition to personal details.
  • Times Car said customer notifications will be sent in stages, while its car-sharing services continue to operate normally.

Japanese car-sharing company Times Car says someone got into its systems and took personal information connected to about 6.6 million current and former customers, including some business-account users. The information may include names, addresses, contact details, driver’s license information and images, and account passwords stored in a form the company says cannot be read back. Credit card information was not affected, but affected people could face convincing fake emails, text messages, or phone calls using their stolen details, so Times Car is warning customers to be cautious.

US soldier gets 70 months in prison for extorting 10 tech, telecom firms

Former U.S. Army soldier Cameron Wagenius was sentenced to 70 months in prison and ordered to pay nearly $295,000 for hacking and extorting at least 10 U.S. technology and telecom companies. He and accomplices stole credentials and sensitive data, threatened leaks, and attempted to extort at least $1 million.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Former U.S. Army soldier Cameron John Wagenius was sentenced to 70 months in prison and ordered to pay $294,978 in restitution for hacking and extorting U.S. technology and telecommunications companies.
  • 02While on active duty, Wagenius and his accomplices used a credential-guessing tool called SSH Brute and shared stolen login details through Telegram to access victim networks.
  • 03The group threatened to publish stolen data on BreachForums and XSS.is, sold some of the data, and attempted to extort at least $1 million from victim data owners.
  • 04Two alleged accomplices, Connor Riley Moucka and John Erin Binns, were accused of stealing terabytes of data from more than 165 organizations using Snowflake cloud storage services.
  • 05Following breaches linked to the Snowflake incidents, Snowflake announced it would enforce multi-factor authentication and require customer passwords to be at least 14 characters long.

Former U.S. Army soldier Cameron John Wagenius, known online as “kiberphant0m” and “cyb3rph4nt0m,” was sentenced to 70 months in prison for hacking and extorting at least 10 U.S. technology and telecommunications companies between April 2023 and December 2024. He was also ordered to pay $294,978 in restitution. Wagenius had pleaded guilty to charges involving unlawful transfer of confidential phone records, aggravated identity theft, wire-fraud conspiracy, and computer-fraud extortion.

While on active duty, Wagenius and accomplices used the SSH Brute tool, which he helped develop, to steal network login credentials and used Telegram to share credentials and plan activity. The group threatened to publish stolen information on BreachForums and XSS.is, sold some stolen data, and used data in further fraud including SIM-swapping. They attempted to extort at least $1 million from data owners, while two alleged accomplices were also tied to thefts from more than 165 organizations using Snowflake services. Following the Snowflake-linked incidents, Snowflake announced that it would enforce multi-factor authentication and require passwords of at least 14 characters.

  • The case shows that stolen customer data was used for more than ransom demands: the conspirators also sold some of it and used it to support SIM-swapping fraud.
  • The alleged activity occurred while Wagenius was on active duty in the U.S. Army, and the group coordinated credential sharing and attack planning through Telegram.
  • The Snowflake-related incidents prompted Snowflake to require multi-factor authentication and passwords of at least 14 characters, illustrating a direct security-policy response to large-scale account compromises.

Former U.S. Army soldier Cameron Wagenius was sentenced to nearly six years in prison for breaking into at least 10 U.S. technology and phone companies, stealing customer information, and demanding money to keep it private. He and others used stolen account logins to access company systems, then threatened to post the data online or sell it. The case matters because thefts linked to this group affected hundreds of millions of customers at companies including AT&T, Ticketmaster, and Santander, exposing how stolen personal records can be used for further fraud.

CISA orders feds to patch exploited Citrix flaws by Wednesday

CISA ordered U.S. federal agencies to patch actively exploited Citrix NetScaler RCE flaws CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 by September 30. Organizations with affected internet-facing appliances should assess for compromise and preserve forensic evidence before updating.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CISA added CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog and directed U.S. federal civilian agencies to secure vulnerable Citrix appliances by September 30.
  • 02Citrix confirmed that both NetScaler flaws are being exploited in zero-day attacks and urged customers to install the relevant updates immediately.
  • 03The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely run code on affected NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances; the second flaw requires DTLS, which is enabled by default on VPN virtual servers.
  • 04Citrix provided generic indicators of compromise through NetScaler Console but warned they may have limited forensic value and may not identify actual compromises.
  • 05CERT-EU strongly advised EU organizations to assess internet-facing appliances running affected builds for signs of compromise.

CISA has ordered U.S. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies to secure vulnerable Citrix NetScaler appliances by September 30 after adding CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog. Citrix confirmed on Sunday that both flaws are being actively exploited in zero-day attacks and urged customers to install updates immediately. The Dutch National Cyber Security Center had reportedly warned organizations about the two critical flaws before CVE identifiers were assigned. CISA said that, where possible, organizations should look for signs of compromise before patching.

Both vulnerabilities can let an unauthenticated attacker remotely run code on affected NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway deployments. CVE-2026-88771 affects deployments using default configurations, while CVE-2026-88772 requires DTLS to be enabled; Citrix says DTLS is enabled by default on VPN virtual servers. Citrix made generic indicators of compromise available through NetScaler Console, but warned that they may have limited forensic value and fail to identify actual compromises. It advised potentially affected customers to retain experienced forensic investigators, while CISA cautioned that updates may result in lost forensic visibility.

Shadowserver tracks more than 23,000 internet-exposed IP addresses with NetScaler fingerprints, though the article notes this does not show how many are honeypots, patched, or vulnerable under their configurations. CERT-EU strongly advised EU organizations to perform a compromise assessment on internet-facing appliances running affected builds. The two flaws follow several other Citrix vulnerabilities exploited this year, and CISA has flagged 26 actively exploited Citrix vulnerabilities since November 2021, including six used by ransomware gangs.

  • Organizations should check for signs of compromise and preserve forensic evidence before applying updates, because Citrix and CISA warn that updating may reduce forensic visibility.
  • Citrix’s supplied indicators of compromise may miss real intrusions, so the company recommends retaining experienced forensic investigators for potentially compromised deployments.
  • The second flaw affects deployments with DTLS enabled, and Citrix says DTLS is enabled by default on VPN virtual servers, making configuration review especially important.
  • More than 23,000 NetScaler-fingerprinted internet-facing IP addresses are visible to Shadowserver, although the article notes that the count does not establish which systems remain vulnerable or patched.

U.S. officials told federal agencies to quickly update Citrix NetScaler systems after attackers began using two newly discovered flaws to take control of them without logging in. The affected systems help organizations manage network traffic and remote connections, and more than 23,000 similar devices are visible on the internet. This matters because a successful break-in could let criminals disrupt services or gain a foothold in an organization’s network, so Citrix customers are being urged to check whether they were already affected before installing updates.

JadePuffer agentic AI attacks target Azure, destroy cloud resources

Microsoft observed JadePuffer (Storm-3168) using compromised Azure service principals in agent-driven attacks to map tenant resources, steal storage keys, and rapidly delete more than 100 storage accounts and other cloud assets. Resource locks and account protections limited some damage, while a service-principal credential may have been exposed publicly on GitHub.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft observed two June attacks by JadePuffer, tracked as Storm-3168, against Azure tenants using two compromised service principals from the same tenant.
  • 02The attackers mapped cloud resources, retrieved Azure Storage account keys, and attempted destructive actions against more than 100 storage accounts, Key Vaults, Function Apps, virtual machines, and App Services within seven minutes.
  • 03Most targeted Azure Storage accounts were deleted, but Azure resource locks and storage account-level protections prevented some deletions.
  • 04Attempts to delete Azure SQL databases and remove Azure Site Recovery protection locks failed because the attackers used an unsupported API version and could not remove the recovery locks.
  • 05About 30 minutes after the deletion attempts, Storm-3168 made more than 30 requests for storage account keys, most of which succeeded; Microsoft noted that credentials for one service principal had appeared in a public GitHub issue before the attacks.

Microsoft Security Research observed two June attacks in which JadePuffer, tracked as Storm-3168, used compromised Azure service principals to map cloud resources, collect storage account keys, and delete resources. The destructive activity lasted seven minutes and targeted more than 100 Azure Storage accounts, as well as Key Vaults, Function Apps, virtual machines, and App Services. Most targeted storage accounts were deleted, though Azure resource locks and storage account-level protections prevented some deletions.

The attackers used one compromised service principal for reconnaissance and another for discovery, destructive actions, and credential collection. Attempts to delete Azure SQL databases failed because an unsupported API version was used, and attempts to remove Azure Site Recovery protection locks also failed. About 30 minutes later, Storm-3168 made more than 30 requests for storage account keys, most of which succeeded; Microsoft noted that credentials for one service principal had appeared in a public GitHub issue before the attacks, although the initial access method was not confirmed.

  • Azure resource locks and storage account-level protections prevented some storage-account deletions, showing that these controls limited the observed destructive activity.
  • The attacker used separate compromised service principals for reconnaissance and for discovery, credential collection, and destructive actions, dividing tasks between two identities in the same tenant.
  • The destructive activity targeted multiple Azure service types rather than storage alone, including Key Vaults, Function Apps, virtual machines, and App Services.
  • Deletion attempts against Azure SQL databases failed because the attacker used an unsupported API version, and attempts to remove Azure Site Recovery locks also failed.
  • A credential for one of the compromised service principals appeared in a public GitHub issue before the attacks, although Microsoft could not determine the exact initial-access method.

JadePuffer is a ransomware group that used stolen access to Microsoft Azure accounts to look through a company’s online resources, collect storage keys, and delete important data services. Microsoft saw the group target more than 100 online storage accounts, along with backup, database, app, and virtual computer services. This matters because deleting cloud resources can quickly disrupt an organization and make recovery difficult, although some protections prevented part of the damage.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This reports observed, destructive attacks by the named JadePuffer/Storm-3168 actor against Azure tenants, including deletion of more than 100 storage accounts and theft of storage keys. It is broadly relevant to organizations using Azure service principals and cloud-hosted storage, backups, databases, and application services.

80,000+ Organizations Had AI Logins Stolen: From Shadow AI to LLMjacking

SOCRadar reports that infostealer logs contain AI-service credentials and sessions tied to more than 80,000 corporate domains, with ChatGPT/OpenAI accounts dominating its sampled enterprise dataset. Stolen AI sessions can expose sensitive prompt histories, bypass MFA through session-cookie replay, enable abuse of connected automation tools, and facilitate API-key theft and LLMjacking.
KEY POINTS
  • 01SOCRadar analyzed more than one million infostealer records tied to AI services across more than 80,000 corporate domains and closely examined 482 major enterprises.
  • 02The 482 enterprises had 5,434 stealer-log records tied to 1,500 distinct corporate email addresses, and 295 of the companies appeared in records from the preceding 90 days.
  • 03ChatGPT or OpenAI sessions appeared at 358 of the 482 companies and accounted for roughly 90% of the study’s records.
  • 04The article says stolen AI sessions can expose conversation histories, remain usable without a password prompt, enable misuse of connected automation services, and allow API keys to be billed to or resold from the victim.
  • 05The article recommends placing AI platforms behind single sign-on with short-lived sessions, rotating API keys, monitoring for reused sessions, and identifying unmanaged AI accounts.

SOCRadar’s AI Identity Exposure Report examined more than one million infostealer records associated with AI services across more than 80,000 corporate domains. It narrowed its analysis to 482 established enterprises, finding 5,434 records linked to 1,500 corporate email addresses; 295 of those companies appeared in records from the previous 90 days. ChatGPT or OpenAI sessions were found at 358 of the 482 companies and represented about 90% of the records, while Zapier, Notion, Hugging Face, Replit, Lovable, and ElevenLabs appeared less often.

The article says a stolen AI login can expose stored chat histories containing source code, customer information, contracts, and unreleased plans. Stolen active-session cookies can be replayed without a password prompt, while connected automation accounts can carry existing permissions into CRM, email, and storage systems; stolen API keys can also be used or resold for paid AI capacity. It recommends putting AI platforms behind single sign-on with short-lived sessions, rotating and monitoring API keys, detecting reused sessions, and identifying unmanaged AI accounts tied to corporate domains.

  • The report interprets ChatGPT’s overwhelming presence in the dataset as evidence of employees using unapproved AI accounts with work email addresses, rather than as a comparison of vendors’ security.
  • Changing an account password may not remove an intruder if the attacker has already stolen an active session token, so the article recommends treating a stealer-log appearance as an infected-device incident rather than only a password-reset issue.
  • Connected automation accounts can extend the impact beyond the AI service itself because an attacker could use existing permissions to create scheduled workflows that remove data from other business systems.
  • The article emphasizes that AI API keys can create both data-access and financial risk, since stolen keys may be used for paid AI capacity or resold to others.

A SOCRadar report found stolen login details for AI services linked to more than 80,000 work domains, including 482 large companies it examined closely. Employees’ ChatGPT accounts appeared most often, but accounts for services such as Zapier, Notion, Hugging Face, and Replit were also found. Someone who buys a stolen AI login may be able to read past chats containing company information, use paid AI services at the victim’s expense, or access other connected work tools. This matters because a single infected personal or unmanaged computer can expose business data and give criminals a way into accounts that may already be signed in.

This sponsored report provides concrete exposure statistics from infostealer logs and useful detail on risks from stolen AI sessions and API keys. However, it is primarily a broad trend and best-practice piece rather than reporting a newly actionable incident requiring immediate response.

watchTowr analyzed CVE-2026-88771, an actively exploited pre-authentication command-injection vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances that affects default configurations. The article states that an unauthenticated attacker can cause arbitrary commands to run as root by placing crafted text into NetScaler logs. Citrix addressed this flaw alongside seven other vulnerabilities in bulletin CTX697096, including CVE-2026-88772, which the article also identifies as exploited in the wild.

The vulnerable ns_monuploadd_err.pl script extracted a supposed NSPPE core-file name from logs using shell pipelines, then inserted that value into a later shell command. Crafted log content containing shell control characters could therefore turn the later find command into command execution; the article says login fields, failed-login data, rate-limit events, request parameters, and User-Agent headers can reach relevant logs. Citrix’s fix restricts the expected NSPPE name and numeric process ID, invokes find without a shell, and validates returned paths; the article lists fixed releases including NetScaler 14.1-73.37 and 13.1-64.23.

  • Because the vulnerable script can run only as part of a periodic process, normal exploitation may take up to 24 hours to execute unless its processing is forced.
  • The patch uses two independent protections: it builds the core filename from narrowly restricted log fields and runs find through separate arguments rather than a shell command.
  • The advisory includes seven additional flaws, including CVE-2026-88772, which the article says was also exploited in the wild and affects DTLS-enabled VPN virtual servers by default.

The article examines a serious flaw in Citrix NetScaler, equipment many large organizations use to manage website traffic and employee remote access. An unauthenticated outsider could send specially crafted information that gets written into the device’s logs and later causes it to run the outsider’s commands with full control of the device. Microsoft reported that the NeedyMantis malware family has been used to maintain long-term access in a small number of targeted intrusions since at least October 2025. Affected organizations include telecommunications companies, universities, medical nonprofits, intergovernmental organizations, and government contractors. Microsoft tracks one user of the malware as Storm-3069, whose activity it assesses appears to originate in China, while noting that multiple groups may use NeedyMantis and that no specific nation-state actor has been identified.

NeedyMantis is delivered as a bundle containing a legitimate program, a malicious DLL file named after one the program normally loads, and an encrypted archive. When the legitimate program runs, it loads the malicious DLL, which extracts later components that communicate with a command-and-control server over HTTPS before switching to WebSocket. Microsoft published file hashes, file paths, the C2 domain corp.tripswithengine[.]com, and the hard-coded firefox/21.0 user agent to help organizations identify activity, but cautioned that its hunting queries search only the previous seven days and that a normal Poedit WinSparkle.dll file alone does not prove infection.

  • Microsoft’s published hunting queries look back only seven days, so running them unchanged would not detect activity from the malware samples first seen in October 2025 or May 2026.
  • Although Microsoft connected Storm-3069 to the DAEMON Tools supply-chain campaign, it has not observed NeedyMantis being delivered through the tampered DAEMON Tools installers.
  • After initially connecting over HTTPS, NeedyMantis switches to a WebSocket connection that operators can use to load or unload additional modules and send data to them.

The activity appears linked to China-based interests, though Microsoft has not identified a specific government-backed group.   • 03Each agent should have a distinct identity and should use federated workload identity with short-lived, automatically rotated credentials rather than shared accounts or embedded secrets.
  • 04Agent authority can be limited through task-scoped grants, tool allowlists, data boundaries, and human approval for high-consequence actions.

The article presents a practical identity and access management framework for AI agents operating across enterprise systems. It argues that agents should be managed as non-human identities with a named human owner, defined purpose, limited authority, expiration, and ongoing monitoring. Traditional identity systems can manage provisioning and sign-in controls, but they often do not reveal what an agent actually did after gaining access to an application.

The framework calls for distinct agent identities, short-lived and automatically rotated credentials, and delegated access that keeps the agent’s identity separate from a user’s authority. It recommends task-scoped permissions, tool allowlists, data boundaries, and human approval for high-consequence actions to limit agent behavior. The article emphasizes runtime visibility across applications and infrastructure so organizations can compare intended tasks with actual actions, revoke authority quickly when behavior diverges, and generate telemetry-backed audit evidence.

  • An identity-provider-only view can make an agent appear well governed even when its meaningful actions, such as exporting customer data or changing entitlements, occur only inside connected applications.
  • When an agent acts for a user, preserving the difference between the agent's own identity and the authority lent by the user is important; reusing a user's session token removes that distinction.
  • Framework evaluations should prioritize how quickly authority can be revoked and whether the system produces evidence of actual behavior, not just whether access was provisioned correctly.
  • Many enterprises will need a combined approach: extend existing IAM for lifecycle governance, build in-application enforcement, and add tooling for discovering identities and verifying runtime behavior.
  • Agent-to-agent task delegation can propagate authority through chains that no human approved step by step, making identity, scope, expiration, and human accountability necessary at every link.

The article explains how organizations should manage AI assistants that can sign in to business systems, use tools, and act for people. These assistants can access customer records, supplier information, or infrastructure controls, so companies need to know who is responsible for each one, limit what it can do, and remove access when needed. The main risk is that ordinary identity systems may show what access was granted but not what an AI assistant actually did after signing in. Continuous records of its actions can help organizations catch overreach and provide proof for audits.

Researchers at ThreatDown disclosed Carbonato, a botnet that targets Docker services exposed without authentication on port 2375. It spreads by scanning nearby networks every five minutes for additional exposed Docker daemons. On compromised hosts, it launches privileged containers that can run commands on the underlying system.

Carbonato establishes remote access through a reverse SSH tunnel to a relay in Costa Rica, installs an SSH server using the operators’ key, and uses cron jobs and watchdog scripts to maintain persistence. It then installs the open-source Hermes Agent framework and replaces its SOUL.md persona file with instructions to receive tasks over Telegram, preserve access, and collect AI API keys and other credentials. The article describes Carbonato as part of a broader rise in the use of AI agents to automate reconnaissance, exploitation, post-compromise activity, and data theft.

Researchers found a new program called Carbonato that breaks into poorly protected Docker systems, then spreads to nearby systems and gives its operators remote control through Telegram. It installs an AI assistant that can receive instructions, run commands, and look for valuable login details and AI service keys. This affects organizations whose Docker services are exposed without a password, and it shows how criminals can use AI to carry out harmful work faster and with less hands-on effort.

RatHat Android Malware Console Uses Gemini to Identify Higher-Value Victims

  • 01Cleafy traced nearly 100 deployments of RatHat’s web-based control console since April 2026, which it said is consistent with a malware-as-a-service model in which customers operate separate copies.
  • 02The latest RatHat console uses Google’s Gemini model to estimate victims’ bank balances from stolen text messages and sort infected phones into high-value and mid-value groups.

  • 05The Go program can remain active after the victim removes the RatHat app until the phone restarts, and Zimperium found it can reinstall the app and re-enable Accessibility access.

Cleafy reported that RatHat operators use a web console to build Android banking malware and manage infected phones, tracing nearly 100 console deployments since April 2026. The latest console uses Google’s Gemini model to estimate victims’ bank balances from stolen text messages and categorize devices as high- or mid-value targets. Cleafy said the model is used to help operators decide which victims deserve attention, not to transfer money.

RatHat is distributed through text messages and online ads leading to third-party download sites, then requests Accessibility access to control the phone. It can enable wireless debugging and connect through Android Debug Bridge, giving operators a shell outside the app’s usual permissions; a separately deployed Go program can stream screens and send taps without a recording icon on supported Android versions. The program may remain active after the app is removed until the phone restarts, and Zimperium found it can reinstall the app and re-enable Accessibility access.

  • RatHat uses Gemini in two distinct ways: the control console prioritizes victims based on estimated balances, while the app on the phone can ask Gemini where to tap when its prewritten instructions fail.
  • The console’s scheduled rebuild feature produces new versions of the same malware every hour, an approach Cleafy said is intended to evade tools that identify known files by their digital fingerprint.
  • Although the malware’s Android app has changed little since late 2025, its operator console was replaced several times in 2026, with BlackCat Remote Control Management and Panda Workshop V5 and V6 sharing the same underlying code.
  • The more covert screen-viewing tools do not work on Android 14 and later, where RatHat must rely on its app-based screen capture that requests permission and displays a recording indicator.
  • After the separate Go component is deployed, its minicap and minitouch files can be found under /data/local/tmp, and Cleafy recommended monitoring processes that run as Android’s shell user, UID 2000.

RatHat is an Android banking scam app that can steal text messages and passwords entered into fake bank sign-in screens. Its operators use Google’s Gemini AI to estimate which infected people may have the most money, so they can focus their effort on those victims. The app can also gain unusually broad control of a phone, letting criminals view the screen and tap buttons remotely, sometimes without showing a recording notice. This matters because people who install apps from text-message links, ads, or unofficial download sites could have their banking information and phone activity exposed.

CISA added two critical Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after receiving reports of active exploitation worldwide. Both flaws have a CVSS score of 9.5. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies were directed to apply fixes by September 30, 2026.

CVE-2026-88771 can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands, while CVE-2026-88772 can allow remote code execution or denial of service when DTLS is enabled, which is the default on VPN virtual servers. Citrix released fixes for affected NetScaler 14.1, 13.1, FIPS, and NDcPP versions and made indicators of compromise available through NetScaler Console. watchTowr Labs reported that CVE-2026-88771 involves attacker-influenced log data being passed into a shell command by a NetScaler Perl script, allowing pre-authentication command injection as root.

  • CVE-2026-88772 has a narrower exposure condition than CVE-2026-88771 because it requires DTLS to be enabled, but DTLS is enabled by default on VPN virtual servers.

  • For suspected compromise, Citrix recommends treating the appliance as a possible pivot point by investigating every server and system it connected to, not only the appliance itself.
  • watchTowr Labs found that CVE-2026-88771 can be triggered through a pre-authentication login request because attacker-controlled data written into logs is later incorporated into a shell command.
  • When restoring from a known-good NetScaler backup, Citrix recommends rotating local-account passwords and Key Encryption Keys and replacing restored SSL certificates.

U.S. cyber officials say criminals are actively taking advantage of two serious weaknesses in Citrix NetScaler systems used by organizations to manage network access. The flaws can let an outsider run commands on an affected device without logging in, potentially giving them control of it or knocking it offline. Organizations using NetScaler ADC or Gateway should install Citrix’s fixes quickly, because a compromised device could also expose other systems it connects to.

Microsoft said the threat actor JADEPUFFER, which it tracks as Storm-3168, used compromised service principals to carry out destructive activity in an Azure environment over about 18 hours in early June 2026. Two service principals associated with the same tenant were used, with one largely conducting reconnaissance and the other performing discovery, collecting credentials, and executing destructive actions. The activity targeted Azure Storage Accounts, SQL databases, Key Vaults, Function Apps, recovery protection locks, Virtual Machines, and App Services.

The attackers spent nearly 16 hours performing more than 300 read operations to enumerate subscriptions, resource groups, virtual machines, and other resources before launching destructive and credential-collection activity. They attempted more than 100 storage-account deletions in about seven minutes, and Microsoft said most targeted storage accounts were successfully deleted. Attempts to delete Azure SQL databases failed because the attackers used an unsupported API version, while resource locks and storage-level deletion protection prevented some storage-account deletions.

Microsoft observed that the affected service principal’s client ID, client secret, and tenant ID had previously appeared in plaintext in a public GitHub issue and remained accessible through its edit history after being removed. Microsoft assessed the activity as ransomware-aligned because it included deletion of resources and backup- and recovery-related protections, although it observed no ransom note or successful data theft.   • The attempted Azure SQL database deletions failed because the attackers used an unsupported API version for that Azure SQL resource type.

Microsoft says a group called JADEPUFFER used leaked access details to enter one organization’s Microsoft Azure account and try to delete its online data, applications, databases, and recovery tools. The access details had reportedly been posted in a public GitHub issue and were still visible in its edit history after removal. Many storage accounts were deleted, although some were protected by safeguards that prevented deletion. The case matters because criminals may increasingly use AI to coordinate faster, wider damage in cloud services, making it harder for affected organizations to recover.

Four mailboxes at a UAE-based food import and distribution group received fake internal payroll notices with personalized PDF attachments, and all messages were quarantined. The PDFs claimed a compensation adjustment was effective at 2026-05-07 11:50:13, while the stored file was created one second later and the email was timestamped one second after that. This timing sequence indicated that the stated effective date was likely drawn from the document generator’s clock rather than a genuine business decision.

The document exposed other template failures: it used the recipient’s email address for both employee identification and document reference, greeted a shared mailbox as if it were a person, and contained an unmatched quotation mark consistent with an unresolved merge field. It instructed recipients to scan a verification code to review and electronically sign documentation, but the PDF contained no links, scripts, automatic actions, or recovered code destination. The attachment was technically clean and fully readable, so automated scanning found no executable payload; a human report produced the malicious verdict, illustrating how social-engineering lures can evade controls focused on files and links.

  • A salary effective date rendered to the second, followed by PDF creation and email transit within two seconds, provided a strong clue that the stated business date was copied from an automated document generator’s clock rather than a genuine compensation decision.

  • A PDF can be clean from a file-scanning perspective yet still serve as a phishing lure when it directs the recipient to continue the interaction by scanning a code with another device.
  • Passing sender-authentication checks at the final delivery hop did not establish that the message’s full history was trustworthy, because the earlier recorded origin results showed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC failures and the ARC chain was broken.
  • The incident demonstrates that human reporting can be decisive for detecting social-engineering messages when automated attachment analysis finds no executable content, links, or scripts.

Four email accounts at a food import and distribution company in the United Arab Emirates received fake salary-adjustment notices with a PDF attachment, and all were quarantined after someone reported them. The document looked official but used the recipient’s email address where an employee name should be and gave a salary effective time down to the second—the same clock time used to create and send the file. It told recipients to scan a verification code to sign paperwork, potentially moving them to a phone or other route outside normal email checks. The case shows that convincing fraud can contain no harmful software or clickable link, so noticing implausible details and reporting suspicious messages can stop it.

Netskope describes how its One Data Lineage feature reconstructs a file’s path when it is downloaded, renamed, edited, and uploaded to another location. Application-specific IDs do not persist across services, filenames can change, and content hashes may change after edits or even during uploads. As a result, network-based monitoring can observe a download and an upload without being able to prove they involve the same file.

The product ranks available evidence, prioritizing events that identify both source and destination, followed by shared application object IDs and more limited content, name, location, and time matches. It avoids treating matching content alone as proof of file movement and marks uncertain connections separately from proven lineage. Netskope combines inline network visibility, SaaS application API activity, and endpoint events such as local renames, edits, copies, and transfers to create a continuous record; endpoint events are currently in beta for incident-triggered lineage.

  • A file’s content hash may change even without a user edit because some applications alter its bytes during upload, making hash-based tracking unreliable across services.
  • A complete-looking lineage graph can be less useful than an incomplete one if relaxed matching rules create false links between unrelated files.
  • Edits and renames are retained in a file location’s timeline rather than creating separate graph nodes, preserving investigative detail without cluttering the movement graph.
  • Endpoint visibility is specifically necessary when the evidence connecting a download and a later upload was created entirely on the device and never crossed the network.

The article describes Netskope’s way of following a file after someone downloads it, changes its name and contents on a computer, and uploads it elsewhere. This matters because ordinary network monitoring may see the download and later upload but cannot prove they are the same file after those changes. By also recording what happens on the computer itself, such as renaming, editing, copying, or moving files to a USB drive, the system can provide a more complete record for people investigating how sensitive data moved.

Elastic and Sublime Security integrate email-quarantine telemetry with endpoint, identity, and network signals so agentic workflows can correlate phishing campaigns and coordinate response. Teams can use human-approved or automated actions, including quarantining related emails across mailboxes based on endpoint malware hashes.
KEY POINTS
  • 01The native Sublime Security integration sends email detection and quarantine telemetry into Elastic Security alongside endpoint, cloud, network, and identity data.
  • 02Elastic Attack Discovery can correlate Sublime phishing alerts with related security alerts, gather supporting evidence, query raw logs, and present prioritized attack chains mapped to MITRE ATT&CK.
  • 03Elastic Workflows can create an incident case, notify an analyst in Slack with supporting evidence, and require the analyst to approve or reject recommended actions.
  • 04When Elastic Defend identifies malware on a host, an Elastic Workflow can use the file's SHA-256 hash to trigger a Sublime Security blast-radius quarantine across mailboxes.
  • 05The article recommends first deploying Sublime telemetry collection for immediate correlation benefits, then adding two-way response actions after deciding which actions require analyst approval.

Elastic’s native integration with Sublime Security brings email detections and quarantine actions into Elastic Security, where they can be reviewed alongside endpoint, identity, cloud, and network activity. The article illustrates how a quarantined phishing email and a suspicious PowerShell command five minutes later may individually seem resolved or insignificant but together can indicate a campaign. It argues that consolidating these signals reduces investigation handoffs and helps defenders respond at the speed of automated phishing and vulnerability chaining.

Elastic Attack Discovery can examine related alerts, entity context, and raw logs to assemble evidence-grounded attack chains mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. Elastic Workflows can open a case, send evidence to an analyst through Slack, and allow the analyst to approve or reject a recommended response. In the reverse direction, when Elastic Defend identifies malware on an endpoint, a workflow can use its SHA-256 hash to trigger a Sublime blast-radius quarantine that removes related messages from mailboxes; teams can choose which actions are automatic and which require human approval.

  • A quarantined phishing email can still be valuable evidence of a broader campaign when it is linked to later endpoint activity, even though the original message never reached an inbox.
  • The integration supports containment in the reverse direction: a malware hash discovered on an endpoint can be used to remove matching messages from every mailbox reached by that file.
  • The article recommends setting autonomy separately for each response action, keeping high-impact mailbox-wide quarantines under human approval while automating lower-impact enrichment or tagging steps.
  • Both Sublime's detection logic and Elastic's detection rules are described as open and tunable, allowing analysts to inspect why an alert or quarantine decision occurred.

The article describes a connection between Elastic and Sublime Security that brings suspicious-email information together with signs of unusual activity on computers, user accounts, and networks. This helps security teams recognize that a blocked phishing email and a suspicious command run minutes later may be parts of the same campaign, rather than unrelated events. It matters because attackers can automate convincing scams and quickly combine multiple weaknesses, while defenders need to act quickly without automatically taking high-impact actions before a person reviews the evidence.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is primarily a vendor product-integration and best-practice article about correlating email and endpoint signals with configurable automated response. It does not report a specific new incident, active exploitation, vulnerability, or urgent patch, so it is low priority despite being relevant to teams using Elastic and Sublime Security.

No Passwords, No Customer Data, Still a Problem

Threat actor TheHatman advertised millions of apparently genuine corporate directory records allegedly taken from Azure and Entra environments, though evidence does not confirm recent breaches of the named organizations. Even without passwords or customer data, directory information enables highly convincing phishing and impersonation, underscoring the need to restrict and monitor identity and application access to Microsoft Graph and directory data.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Between July 31 and August 16, TheHatman posted underground listings claiming to offer about 3.64 million employee records from nine organizations, allegedly obtained from Microsoft Azure and Entra environments.
  • 02Cyera Research found that sample records appeared to contain genuine corporate directory data, including names, work email addresses, telephone numbers, job titles, locations, group memberships, service accounts, and privileged accounts.
  • 03The available evidence does not establish when or where the records were obtained, whether TheHatman personally compromised the named organizations, or whether nine separate cloud environments were breached.
  • 04TCS, Gap, and Vodafone disputed indications of recent compromises, with TCS saying the material appeared to be more than four years old and Vodafone saying customer data was not affected.
  • 05Directory information can help criminals tailor phishing, executive impersonation, and identity-recovery scams, so organizations should review directory-read access and investigate unusual bulk directory-enumeration activity.

In August 2026, a threat actor known as TheHatman advertised approximately 3.6 million employee records allegedly obtained from the Microsoft Azure and Entra environments of nine organizations. Cyera Research found that sampled records appeared to contain genuine corporate directory information, including names, work email addresses, phone numbers, job titles, office locations, group memberships, service accounts, and privileged accounts. However, the available evidence does not establish when or where the data was obtained, whether TheHatman personally accessed the named organizations, or whether nine separate cloud environments were compromised.

Several named organizations disputed evidence of a recent breach, and the article notes that authentic older data can be repackaged and resold. Even without passwords or customer information, directory data can provide criminals with an organizational map that supports targeted phishing, executive impersonation, and requests to reset multi-factor authentication. The article advises organizations to review who and what can read directory information, examine application permissions to Microsoft Graph, reduce standing privileges, and monitor for unusual bulk directory searches or exports.

  • Authentic directory records do not prove a recent breach because old data can be repackaged and resold while remaining accurate.
  • A single privileged application, integration, or service account with directory-reading permissions could provide broad visibility across an environment without requiring separate compromises of every organization named by the seller.
  • Information often treated as non-sensitive, such as reporting lines, job titles, and administrator identities, can become a detailed organizational map for targeted impersonation and phishing.
  • Help-desk and account-recovery processes should not regard knowledge of an employee’s manager, department, title, phone number, or administrator as reliable proof of identity because such details may already be publicly available or circulating on criminal forums.
  • AI agents can create a broader and less predictable exposure than narrowly scoped service accounts because they may retain persistent access to multiple applications, APIs, databases, and cloud resources.

A person using the name TheHatman advertised roughly 3.6 million employee-directory records said to come from nine major organizations, although the evidence does not prove that all of those companies were recently broken into. The records appear genuine and include details such as employee names, work emails, phone numbers, job titles, managers, and administrator accounts, but not passwords or customer information. This still matters because criminals can use those details to create believable fake emails or phone calls that trick employees into giving up access, so companies need to limit how much information any one account or automated tool can see.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

The article covers a specific campaign in which TheHatman advertised millions of apparently genuine corporate directory records, alongside actionable discussion of potential Azure and Entra access paths. Although the claimed breaches are unconfirmed and may involve older data, the exposure has broad relevance because directory data can enable targeted phishing and identity impersonation.

This article explains how Corelight’s network-monitoring data can help find signs that attackers are abusing previously unknown flaws in Citrix NetScaler systems. Detecting suspicious activity quickly matters because an attacker who gets through such a system may be able to reach other company resources.
